mcqs.question: The two-pointer reversal (swap ends, move inward) touches each element how many times, and what does that make its space complexity?
options: Each element is touched once, but a second array is required to hold swapped values
Each element is touched twice, once per pointer pass; O(n) extra space for the two pointers
Each element is touched log n times as the pointers converge; O(log n) space
Each element is part of exactly one swap; O(1) extra space since only two index variables are used
mcqs.explanation: Every element takes part in exactly one swap as the two pointers converge, giving O(n) time; the only extra memory is the two integer index variables, so it's O(1) space with no second array involved.

mcqs.question: Of the three rotate-by-k approaches (extra array, cyclic replacement, reversal trick), which are O(1) extra space?
options: Only the extra-array approach
Cyclic replacement and the reversal trick, but not the extra-array approach
All three achieve O(1) space; they differ only in time complexity
None of them — rotation always requires O(n) auxiliary space
mcqs.explanation: Cyclic replacement and the reversal trick both rearrange the array using only its own storage plus a few index variables. The extra-array approach writes each element into a brand-new array first, which is O(n) space — the one candidates reach for first and the one an in-place constraint rules out.

mcqs.question: Cyclic replacement rotates an array by directly moving each element to its final index. When does a single pass starting at index 0 fail to cover every element?
options: Whenever k is odd
Whenever the array length n is a prime number
Whenever gcd(n, k) is greater than 1, leaving some indices in a separate cycle
Never — one cycle from index 0 always covers the whole array
mcqs.explanation: The cycle starting at index 0 only covers every index when gcd(n, k) equals 1; otherwise the indices split into gcd(n, k) separate cycles, and each one needs to be started explicitly from an uncovered index. Parity of k and primality of n aren't the deciding factor — the gcd is.

mcqs.question: Why must k be reduced with k % n before rotating an array of length n?
options: Because rotating by exactly n returns every element to its original position, so anything beyond n is redundant or out of range
Because reversal-based rotation only works for even k
Because modulo improves the algorithm's time complexity from O(n) to O(log n)
Because array indices in most languages can't exceed the array's length
mcqs.explanation: A rotation by n is a full cycle back to the start, so any k larger than n is equivalent to k % n — skipping the reduction risks an out-of-range access or needless repeated full rotations. It has nothing to do with parity, and it doesn't change the algorithm's time complexity class.

mcqs.question: A candidate writes rotated = arr[k:] + arr[:k] and calls it an in-place rotation. What's wrong with that claim?
options: Slicing and concatenation both build full-size new lists, so this uses O(n) extra space despite reusing the variable name
Nothing — reassigning the result to a variable named arr makes it in-place by definition
It's correct as long as k is less than n/2
It's in-place because Python slices share memory with the original list
mcqs.explanation: In-place refers to the algorithm's peak extra memory, not the variable name the result is assigned to — slicing creates new list objects and concatenation creates a third, all O(n) space. Python slices copy rather than share memory, so this fails the O(1) space bar regardless of k.

mcqs.question: A function rotates an array in place for O(1) space, but the array turns out to be a shared buffer another part of the system still reads expecting the original order. What's the actual risk?
options: None — in-place algorithms are always safe as long as they're O(n) time
The rotation silently corrupts data for every other reader of that shared buffer, since in-place mutation has no notion of "only my caller sees this"
The risk only applies to multi-threaded programs, not single-threaded ones
In-place mutation always throws a runtime error when the array is shared
mcqs.explanation: In-place mutation changes the actual memory backing the array, so any other reference to that same array — another function, a cache, a slice view — sees the mutated data with no error raised. This can happen in single-threaded code too, any time a reference is shared rather than copied; the fix is copying when the array isn't exclusively owned.
